key_findings.finding: At 34 weeks, an estimated fetal weight (or abdominal circumference) below the 10th percentile meets the SMFM definition of fetal growth restriction, even when anatomy and amniotic fluid are normal; constitutional smallness remains a clinical possibility, especially with two constitutionally short parents, but cannot be established from parental stature alone.

source_tools.relevance: SMFM Consult Series #52 definition and diagnostic framework
Evidence distinguishing SGA as a biometric category from growth restriction and noting that many small fetuses have no adverse outcomes
Review contrasting growth-restricted and constitutionally small infants

key_findings.finding: The most appropriate next evaluation is umbilical artery Doppler velocimetry, followed by serial surveillance if FGR is diagnosed. SMFM recommends serial UA Doppler assessment for deterioration; weekly assessment is suggested for decreased end-diastolic velocity or EFW below the 3rd percentile, and 2–3 times weekly assessment for absent end-diastolic velocity.

source_tools.relevance: Direct SMFM recommendations on serial and frequency-adjusted UA Doppler surveillance

key_findings.finding: Repeat ultrasound is useful for growth trajectory and amniotic fluid, but not sooner than about 2–3 weeks for reliable interval growth (often every 3–4 weeks); it should not substitute for UA Doppler when placental insufficiency is suspected. Weekly NST/CTG is generally appropriate for stable FGR with reassuring UA Doppler; BPP is an alternative or adjunct when NST is nonreactive, technically limited, or additional concern exists, not a replacement for UA Doppler.

source_tools.relevance: SMFM guidance supports serial UA Doppler and cardiotocographic surveillance; published descriptions of close surveillance include weekly NST/BPP, weekly UA Doppler, and growth scans every 2–4 weeks
Study summary describing common close-surveillance components and growth-scan interval

key_findings.finding: Routine MCA Doppler/cerebroplacental ratio is not the primary surveillance test for an otherwise uncomplicated late-onset small fetus under SMFM guidance; UA Doppler has the strongest management role. MCA may be considered selectively by a maternal-fetal-medicine specialist, particularly when late-onset placental insufficiency or fetal anemia/brain-sparing is suspected, but an isolated normal MCA should not reassure against abnormal placental resistance.

source_tools.relevance: SMFM Consult Series emphasizes UA Doppler-based management; the available evidence describes MCA/CPR as outcome predictors in selected very small fetuses rather than the core first-line test
Study of CPR and uterine artery Doppler in very small term fetuses

key_findings.finding: At 34 weeks with normal fluid and anatomy, normal UA Doppler and reassuring testing generally support expectant management with surveillance rather than immediate delivery; delivery is usually planned around 38–39 weeks for isolated FGR with normal UA Doppler, earlier for worsening Doppler or testing. SMFM recommends heightened surveillance, corticosteroids, and consideration of delivery for reversed end-diastolic flow; absent/reversed flow requires specialist management and substantially earlier delivery windows.

source_tools.relevance: SMFM recommendations for abnormal UA Doppler, including hospitalization/corticosteroids/intensified cardiotocography with reversed flow
Guideline-oriented evidence describing surveillance and timing-of-delivery frameworks for FGR

key_findings.finding: Constitutional SGA is favored by stable growth along a low percentile, normal UA Doppler, normal fluid, reassuring NST/BPP, and absence of maternal/placental disease; FGR is more concerning when there is falling growth velocity, low abdominal circumference, oligohydramnios, abnormal UA Doppler, hypertension/preeclampsia, or abnormal fetal testing. Because these features are not fully known here, the evidence is insufficient to label this fetus definitively constitutional at 34 weeks.

source_tools.relevance: Evidence that a substantial proportion of small fetuses are not associated with adverse outcomes and that abnormal Doppler/placental malperfusion helps identify higher-risk phenotypes
